newsitem.title: JAPAN: TIFFE Euroyen ends down on swap-rate rises.
newsitem.headline: TIFFE Euroyen ends down on swap-rate rises.

text.p: The key December three-month Euroyen deposit-rate contract ended the day session on Thursday weaker in response to steep rises in interest-rate swaps (IRS).

Bankers said a 100 billion to 200 billion yen deal was made with two-year IRS. A Japanese bank paid a fixed rate, while foreign accounts received it, pushing up IRS rates across the curve in an otherwise quiet market. The two-year IRS was at 0.98-1.02 percent at 0710 GMT up from Wednesday's 0.93-0.97.
December opened at the day's low of 99.06 in response to remarks made by a senior Japanese Finance Ministry official overnight.

Eisuke Sakakibara, director-general of the ministry's International Finance Bureau, said on Wednesday that although monetary policy was in the hands of the Bank of Japan, there was political pressure to raise the official discount rate.

"Some politicians have called for a rise in the official discount rate. It is true that there is an atmosphere among politicians to raise the official discount rate," he told currency dealers at a foreign exchange conference.

A foreign media report quoted a foreign exchange dealer who attended the conference as saying that Sakakibara had said Japan would consider raising interest rates from June through August after examining economic indicators for April to June.
"The media report knocked down the December (Euroyen) at the outset as it reignited fears of a credit tightening," said a trader at a European bank.

Sentiment was depressed further as the Bank of Japan (BOJ) let the bank reserve fall to a surplus of around 90 billion yen on Thursday through its regular money market operation, from 200 billion yen on Wednesday.

However, the early morning depression was somewhat alleviated by the announcement of slow money supply growth for March that revived expectations that the central bank would maintain its easy monetary stance at least for a while.

The BOJ said Japan's broadly defined money supply average of M2 plus certificates of deposit (CDs) grew a preliminary 2.7 percent in March from a year earlier. It grew a revised three percent year-on-year in February.
The 2.7 percent growth was the slowest since October 1995, when it also grew by 2.7 percent.
